# The planning diagram {#sec-plan-diagram}

::: callout-tip
## Objective

Use a hand-drawn diagram as the medium for reaching shared understanding with an
AI agent at the planning stage, keep it in the repository as structured JSON so
it survives as the blueprint later sessions compare the implementation against,
and refine it as the design becomes clearer.
:::

## The goal: think with the agent, not at it

Planning with an agent through chat alone has a characteristic failure.
You describe what you want, the agent restates it convincingly, and you both
proceed, without ever confirming you were picturing the same system.
The misunderstanding is invisible because prose describes components one at a
time, and the thing you disagreed about was how they fit together.

A diagram removes that hiding place.
When the shape is on the canvas, "where does this arrow go?" and "should these
two be separate boxes?" become questions someone can actually ask.
The drawing is not documentation of a decision already made.
It is the surface on which the decision gets made, together.

> The diagram is not the output of planning. It is how planning happens.

This chapter proposes drawing that diagram in
[Excalidraw](https://excalidraw.com/) and committing it to the repository,
for one specific reason: the file is plaintext JSON.
The human sees a picture; the agent reads structured data.
Neither is working from a translation of the other.

## Start rough

The first draft should not be good.

Its only job is to be concrete enough to be wrong in a visible way.
Five boxes and four arrows, drawn in two minutes, will surface more real
disagreement than an hour of careful prose, because the agent can point at a
box and say *I don't know what this is*, or *this needs a connection you
haven't drawn*, or *these two look like the same thing*.

A useful first pass:

1. Sketch the components you are confident exist, and the flow between them.
2. Do not agonize over what you are unsure about. Leave it out, or draw it as a
   single vague box. The gap is information.
3. Ask the agent to read the file and restate the design in its own words:
   what each box is, what each arrow implies, and **what it cannot tell from
   the diagram**.
4. Fix what the restatement got wrong. Usually the diagram was wrong, not the agent.

That last list, what the agent cannot tell, is the most valuable output of the
first round. It is your ambiguity, made visible while it is still cheap to
resolve on a canvas rather than expensive to resolve in code.

Expect two or three rounds. The diagram gets better because you are arguing
about something specific.

> A rough diagram you iterate on beats a polished one you defend.

## Then it becomes the blueprint

Once you and the agent agree on the picture, the drawing changes role.
It stops being a conversation and becomes memory.

This matters because agent sessions are short and the work is not.
The session that plans a component is rarely the session that builds it,
and almost never the session that tests it.
Everything said in the planning conversation is gone by then, but the
committed diagram is still in the repository, and the next session reads it
as a first-class input.

The design intent survives the context window.

That gives every later stage something to check against:

| Stage | What the diagram is used for |
|---|---|
| Implementation | The boundaries to build within; an undrawn dependency is a question, not a liberty |
| Review | Walk each box and arrow against the built system; report what is missing, reversed, or unplanned |
| Testing | Each arrow is an interface worth a test; each boundary is something worth trying to violate |
| Onboarding | A new person, or a fresh session, gets the intended shape in one look |

The review use is the one that earns the file's keep.
The agent can report on each element:

- **Box**: does a corresponding component exist? *present, missing, renamed*
- **Arrow**: does the dependency exist, in that direction? *present, missing, reversed*
- **Boundary**: does anything cross it that should not? *conforms, violated*
- **Built component**: does it appear in the diagram at all? *planned, unplanned*

That last check catches what prose plans never do: components that exist but
were never designed. Scope creep has a shape, and it shows up as boxes on the
canvas that nobody drew.

Every divergence has two valid resolutions: change the code to match the
diagram, or change the diagram because the design genuinely improved during the
build. The agent reports which elements diverged and cites both sides.
Deciding which side was wrong is a human's job.

> The agent reports the divergence. The human decides which side was wrong.

## Keep refining it

The diagram is not finished when the build starts.
Implementation always teaches you something the plan did not know,
and when it does, the change belongs in the drawing before the session ends.

The rule is simple and unforgiving: **a design change is not done until the
diagram is updated.** A drawing that has silently gone stale is worse than no
drawing, because it is a confident description of a system that no longer
exists, and the next session will trust it.

Because the file is JSON, this is checkable.
`git diff` shows which elements were added, removed, or relabelled, so the
diagram accumulates history: when a component appeared, and what else changed
in the same commit.

A working rhythm:

- **Before building**: draw, argue with the agent, commit the agreed version.
- **During building**: when reality diverges, stop and ask which side is right.
- **After building**: run the conformance walk, then commit the corrected diagram
  alongside the code.

## The trade-off you have to master

Here is the part that takes practice.

The diagram has to serve two readers with opposite appetites:

- **A human** needs it simple enough to hold in one look. Past roughly fifteen
  boxes, nobody is really reading it. They are recognizing it. A diagram
  nobody reads cannot catch a mistake.
- **An agent** needs enough detail to verify something. A diagram of three boxes
  labelled *input*, *processing*, *output* is technically a plan, but every
  possible implementation conforms to it, so it can never report a divergence.

Too simple and it is decorative. Too detailed and it is unmaintained.
Both failure modes end the same way: the file stops being consulted.

There is no formula, and the balance shifts by project.
Some guidance that helps:

- **Draw the things that would be expensive to get wrong.**
  Boundaries, ownership, and the direction of dependencies are worth a box.
  Field names and function signatures are not. The agent handles those, and
  they change too fast to keep drawn.
- **Prefer one diagram per concern over one diagram for everything.**
  Several small drawings each stay under the human limit; one large drawing
  fails both readers at once.
- **Detail is earned.** Add a box when its absence caused a real
  misunderstanding, not in anticipation. Diagrams grow well and shrink badly.
- **Every visual property should mean something.** Colour, fill, line weight,
  and shape are channels, and each one spent on decoration is a channel you
  cannot later spend on meaning. If a reader asks what the green boxes have in
  common and the answer is "nothing, it looked nice", the colour is costing
  attention and returning none. Draw in black and white first, then add a
  distinction only when you can say in one sentence what it encodes.
- **Watch the token cost.** Excalidraw JSON is verbose and low in information
  density, roughly 4k to 22k tokens for a typical file. A diagram large enough to
  be an expensive agent input is already too large for a human to check.

Notice that these pressures point the same way.
The size at which a human stops reading is close to the size at which the file
stops being worth its context. That is a convenient coincidence, and a good
sanity check: **if it is getting annoying to send to the agent, it is already
too big to be useful to you.**

Expect to be bad at this at first. Calibration comes from noticing which
divergences your diagram caught and which it missed, and adjusting the
granularity in that direction.

> Simple enough for a human to check. Detailed enough for an agent to verify.
> Finding that line is the skill.

## A worked example

The practice in this chapter is itself drawn as a diagram, in
`diagrams/plan-diagram-workflow.excalidraw` in this repository.

It has four boxes and five arrows:

- **Human draws a rough diagram**, then **Agent restates it and names gaps**,
  with a loop arrow back, labelled *iterate: the first draft is meant to be rough*.
- Then **Blueprint committed as JSON**, the artifact that survives the session.
- Then **Build, review, test vs. the blueprint**, reached *later sessions* on,
  with a loop arrow back to the blueprint labelled
  *divergence? a human decides, then update the diagram*.

Note what is not in it. There is no box for the agent's tools, no arrow for
every file it reads, and no detail about how the comparison is run.
Those are implementation, and drawing them would push the diagram past the
point where anyone checks it. The two loops are the design decisions worth
committing to a picture, so they are what the picture shows.

It is drawn in black and white with a single exception: the blueprint box is
filled. That fill is the one visual property carrying information the layout
does not: three boxes are activities, and one is the artifact those activities
produce and check against. An earlier draft coloured the planning boxes blue and
the checking boxes green, which looked organized but told the reader nothing:
left-to-right order and the *later sessions* label already said which stage was
which.

To display it in the book, open it in Excalidraw and export it as
`.excalidraw.svg` with the scene embedded. That keeps one artifact that both
renders here and stays editable and agent-readable, the same file, not a copy.

## Why Excalidraw

The requirement is a format comfortable enough for a human to sketch in and
structured enough for an agent to parse. Most formats give up one or the other.

| Format | Human sketching | Machine readable | Diffable in git |
|---|---|---|---|
| Whiteboard photo, PNG, PDF | Excellent | No, requires vision | No |
| Mermaid, PlantUML, Graphviz | Poor, it is code | Yes | Yes |
| Visio, Lucidchart, draw\.io | Good | Partly, proprietary or verbose XML | Poorly |
| **Excalidraw** | **Good** | **Yes, plain JSON** | **Yes** |

An `.excalidraw` file is plaintext JSON, so the agent reads it the way it reads
source code, with no vision, screenshot, or OCR step in between:

``` json
{
  "id": "routerText",
  "type": "text",
  "x": 490,
  "y": 373,
  "width": 99,
  "height": 25,
  "text": "Tool Router",
  "containerId": null
}
```

Arrows drawn onto shapes carry `startBinding` and `endBinding` fields naming the
elements they connect, so the file is not just a list of labels.
It is a graph the agent can walk: these are the components, this one depends on
that one, this arrow crosses that boundary.

The deliberately rough, hand-drawn look does useful social work too.
A sketchy diagram reads as provisional and invites correction;
a polished one reads as settled and discourages it.
At the planning stage you want the first.

Practical notes:

- **Export with the scene embedded.** Saving as `.excalidraw.svg` or
  `.excalidraw.png` keeps the full JSON inside the file, so one artifact both
  renders in the book and stays editable and parseable.
- **Edit it in the editor.** The
  [Excalidraw VS Code extension](https://github.com/excalidraw/excalidraw-vscode)
  opens these files in place, so the diagram is updated in the same session as
  the code rather than in a different tool that nobody opens.

## How this relates to the principles

The planning diagram is a concrete instance of the principles in
@sec-principle-overview rather than a separate idea.

- **Inspectable artifacts** (Principle 1). The design becomes readable,
  structured, versioned, and diffable instead of living in a chat transcript.
- **Explicit state** (Principle 2). The committed diagram records what the design
  is now and what it was before, without depending on anyone's memory of a
  planning conversation that has scrolled out of context.
- **Events and rules** (Principle 3). A change to the diagram is an event.
  The rule it triggers is a conformance recheck of the affected components.
- **Tools and evidence** (Principle 4). A conformance finding cites a diagram
  element and a code location. Both sides are inspectable, so the finding can be
  challenged.
- **Human judgment** (Principle 5). The human draws the plan and rules on every
  divergence. The agent prepares the comparison and does not resolve it.

## Limits

**Conformance is not correctness.** A build can match the diagram exactly and
still be wrong, because the diagram was wrong. This practice catches drift from
the plan, not flaws in the plan.

**Diagrams rot.** Keeping diagrams in sync with reality is the known unsolved
problem with diagrams-as-code generally. Putting the file in the repository
makes drift visible in `git diff`, but visibility is not prevention. Only the
habit is.

**The calibration is real work.** The trade-off above is not a detail to settle
once. It is a judgment you re-make on every project, and being bad at it at
first is normal.

## Prior work

This practice combines two threads that already exist separately.

Spec-driven development argues that a structured, human-authored specification
should be the shared source of truth AI executes against
([Thoughtworks](https://www.thoughtworks.com/en-us/insights/blog/agile-engineering-practices/spec-driven-development-unpacking-2025-new-engineering-practices),
[Microsoft](https://developer.microsoft.com/blog/spec-driven-development-ai-native-engineering/)).
Those specs are almost always prose.

The empirical support is more specific. @cervantes2026 evaluated LLM-assisted
code generation with and without architectural documentation as a first-class
input, and found that including it substantially improved architectural
conformance, with an explicit implementation plan further improving functional
correctness and modularity. The claim that a human-authored architecture
artifact makes the generated system conform better is measured, not assumed.

Meanwhile, tooling for agents and Excalidraw runs mostly in the opposite
direction: available skills and MCP servers have the agent *generate* diagrams
and render them for visual self-checking
([excalidraw-diagram-skill](https://github.com/coleam00/excalidraw-diagram-skill),
[mcp_excalidraw](https://github.com/yctimlin/mcp_excalidraw)).
Useful, and evidence that agents handle the format fluently, but a diagram the
agent drew from its own plan cannot audit that plan, because it encodes the same
misunderstanding.

What this chapter proposes is the join: the architecture artifact from the
research is drawn by a human rather than written, used as the medium of the
planning conversation rather than its output, and stored in a format the agent
can parse directly rather than one it has to look at.

## Summary

1. Draw a rough diagram to reach shared understanding with the agent.
   The first draft is a conversation starter, not a specification.
2. Iterate until the agent's restatement matches your intent.
   What it says it *cannot* tell from the diagram is the most useful output.
3. Commit the file as plaintext JSON so the design intent outlives the session
   and becomes the blueprint later sessions read.
4. Compare implementation, review, and testing against it. Divergences are
   reported with evidence from both sides; a human decides which side was wrong.
5. Refine it as the design changes. A design change is not done until the
   diagram is updated.
6. Keep it simple enough for a human to check and detailed enough for an agent
   to verify. That balance is the skill, and it takes time to learn.

> If the plan cannot be inspected, the build cannot be checked against it.
